name: What inspections slow multifamily construction the most?

mainEntity.name: Which inspections or approvals most commonly delay multifamily projects during construction and closeout?
mainEntity.text: Which inspections or approvals most commonly delay multifamily projects during construction and closeout?

acceptedAnswer.text: Multifamily construction can slow down quickly if inspection sequencing is not managed carefully. The biggest pain points are usually foundation, framing, rough mechanical-electrical-plumbing, fire/life-safety, and final inspections. If one trade finishes late or a correction is missed, the next inspection may be delayed even when the rest of the job is ready. In dense local markets, closeout can also take longer because the project may require multiple sign-offs before final occupancy. Utility coordination, sprinkler testing, elevator issues, and life-safety corrections are common closeout bottlenecks. A project can look nearly complete but still be unable to receive final approval if one compliance item remains unresolved. The most efficient builders plan inspections backward from occupancy and verify that each trade is ready before calling for sign-off. Owners should ask how the contractor handles inspection scheduling, punch lists, and correction notices. That process discipline matters as much as the physical construction work, because inspection delays can create carrying costs and push back revenue.
acceptedAnswer.description: The most common delays come from foundation, framing, fire/life-safety, rough MEP, and final inspections. Projects can also stall when corrections are needed after partial sign-off or when one trade is not ready for inspection. Coordination matters because missed sequencing can force reinspection and push back occupancy.
